title: Teaching & Training
text:
I co-lead Open Climate Science for Agriculture, a NASA-funded curriculum that teaches researchers to use NASA satellite data and climate models for agricultural applications in a warming world. The materials are open, Python-based and available in English, French and Arabic.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Research question
How much cropland is there in North Africa’s main cereal-producing regions, and how well do satellite cropland products represent it?

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Motivation
Satellite cropland maps differ in how much cropland they show and in what they count as cropland. In North Africa, independent field-based reference data to test them are scarce.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Geographic scope
The principal cereal-producing regions of Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia, 2023–2024 agricultural season.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Approach
A probability-based field survey across all three countries, combined with design-based area estimation and an assessment of publicly available satellite cropland products.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:

Forthcoming in a manuscript currently in preparation.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text: Accepted · Environmental Research: Climate

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Research question
When does drought become a matter of public, institutional concern?

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Motivation
Drought monitoring records physical anomalies, but not the moment environmental stress becomes publicly recognized and institutionally actionable. Across North Africa, governments periodically organize Islamic rain rituals (Ṣalāt al-Istisqāʾ) in response to water scarcity, and their announcements leave a public record of that moment.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Geographic scope
Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia, 2000–2024.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Approach
A 25-year archival record of 63 state-organized rain rituals, linked to drought indicators over cropland.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Key insight
Institutional recognition of drought follows agricultural drought: it concentrates in the rainfed cropping season and in the main rainfed regions. Rain rituals mark when stress becomes publicly visible; they do not measure drought or its impacts. Full results will appear in the forthcoming article.






In the news. When a Prayer Is Also a Climate Signal. Eos (AGU), 3 December 2025.

How have North African wheat systems evolved, how volatile are they, and how sensitive are they to climate?

Subnational crop statistics are essential for food-security monitoring and for linking climate to agricultural outcomes, but they are scattered and inconsistent. NASA HarvestStat is building the most comprehensive global database of subnational crop production data.

title: Doctoral research
text:
I completed my PhD in Geographical Sciences at the University of Maryland in 2026, directed by Tatiana V. Loboda and mentored by Molly E. Brown. My dissertation, Drought and Agricultural Land-Use Change in North Africa, examined how drought shapes agricultural land use across Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia.
From the start, I wanted to put people in the equation. Satellites show where farmland changes, but not how societies experience drought. So alongside satellite and climate records, I read drought through the moment states publicly recognize it: state-organized rain rituals.
The work also meant going to the fields. Over the 2023–2024 season I drove thousands of kilometres through the cereal belt of all three countries, collecting independent field observations of the region’s farmland.

title: Climate Extremes, Earth Observation & Societal Resilience
text:
Research vision

How do climate extremes generate environmental, infrastructure, and institutional risks, and how can Earth observation and quantitative evidence support more resilient decisions?

title: Climate Extremes, Earth Observation & Societal Resilience
text:
Research directions


Established

Drought & Agricultural Land-Use Change
How drought variability and persistence relate to cropland extent and intensification in drylands, using field surveys, reference datasets and satellite cropland products. Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia.



Established · expanding

Climate Signals & Environmental Governance
When environmental stress becomes institutionally recognized. State-organized rain rituals are studied as observable institutional responses to drought, not as measurements of it.



Emerging

Climate Risk & Critical Infrastructure
Early-stage work at Georgetown on how climate extremes affect critical infrastructure. Details will follow as the work matures; I’m glad to talk with potential collaborators.



Established

Earth Observation & Open Science
Reproducible geospatial analysis, open climate-data tools and remote-sensing training, including a NASA-funded curriculum in three languages.

title: About
text:
Walid Ouaret is an Earth observation scientist and a Postdoctoral Fellow at The Earth Commons Institute, Georgetown University, where he works with Roshanak (Roshi) Nateghi in the SuRGE Lab. His research examines how climate extremes affect agricultural landscapes, critical infrastructure and the institutions that manage environmental risk.
He received his Ph.D. in Geographical Sciences from the University of Maryland, College Park in 2026. His dissertation, Drought and Agricultural Land-Use Change in North Africa, was directed by Tatiana V. Loboda, with mentorship from Molly E. Brown. It combined fieldwork across Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia with satellite, climate and archival records.
Before his doctorate, he worked on landscape and agricultural modeling at INRAE (Montpellier and Paris) and at Wageningen University, and on remote sensing and GIS research at Miami University’s Geospatial Analysis Center. He trained as an agronomist at the École Nationale Supérieure Agronomique in Algiers. He holds master’s degrees from Paris-Saclay University and AgroParisTech, and from the Mediterranean Agronomic Institute of Chania. He co-developed the NASA-funded Open Climate Science for Agriculture curriculum, taught in English, French and Arabic.

title: Agricultural and Environmental Modeling
section: Crop allocation in Tunisian rainfed smallholder systems
text:
Crop allocation in Tunisian rainfed smallholder systems
INRAE Landscape Modeling Team, Montpellier · 2018–2020 · IRD-ARTS grant (PI: Jean-Stéphane Bailly, AgroParisTech)
I collected data through farmer interviews and seasonal crop monitoring in the Lebna watershed using remote sensing. I combined these with expert elicitation to build and validate a crop allocation model for Tunisia’s rainfed smallholder farming systems.

title: Agricultural and Environmental Modeling
text:
Liming trade-offs in western Kenya
Plant Production Systems Group, Wageningen University · 2018
I built a database of field experiments on lime use in maize across Sub-Saharan Africa and ran a trade-off analysis linking yield effects to greenhouse gas emissions and farm income.

Organic and conventional yield synthesis
Global Agronomy Team, UMR Agronomie, INRAE, Paris · 2017
I compiled a global database comparing organic and conventional yields across crop species. I also designed a protocol to elicit quantitative expert knowledge on organic yields.

title: Mapping Agricultural Greenhouses in Algeria
text:
Research question
Where, and how fast, is greenhouse agriculture expanding in Algeria, and can it be mapped reliably from satellite imagery?

title: Mapping Agricultural Greenhouses in Algeria
text:
Scientific motivation
Greenhouse agriculture is a form of intensification that is spreading quickly in Algeria, especially in the southern wilayas. It is poorly documented in agricultural statistics and land-cover products.

title: Mapping Agricultural Greenhouses in Algeria

Algeria.

title: Research agenda
text:
A · Drought & Agricultural Land-Use Change
Established
How drought variability and persistence relate to cropland extent and agricultural intensification in drylands. This direction builds field surveys and reference datasets, assesses remote-sensing cropland products, and examines agricultural vulnerability. Geographic experience: Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia.



Completed · manuscript in preparation

Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation
Field-based cropland area estimation and an independent assessment of satellite cropland maps.




Completed · manuscript in preparation

Drought and Long-Term Cropland Change
Long-term cropland change across the region (2000–2024) and its relationship with drought.




In progress

NASA HarvestStat
Subnational crop production statistics for North Africa, and the evolution, volatility and climate sensitivity of wheat systems.



Published · ongoing

Mapping Agricultural Greenhouses in Algeria
Deep learning on satellite imagery to map rapidly expanding greenhouse agriculture (IEEE M2GARSS 2024).

title: Research agenda
text:
B · Climate Signals & Environmental Governance
Established · expanding
When does environmental stress become publicly recognized and institutionally actionable? This direction studies institutional responses to drought, the role of environmental information in decision-making, climate-risk communication, and how governance is activated under environmental stress. Rain rituals are treated as observable institutional responses, distinct from the physical drought conditions that precede them.



Accepted

Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
When drought becomes publicly and institutionally recognized, read from state-organized rain rituals. Accepted in Environmental Research: Climate.

title: SEEDS: Satellite-Enabled Earth Observation & Digital Solutions for Agriculture
text:
Role: Project Lead · Funding: 6th Grain · Period: 2025–2026
SEEDS puts satellite Earth observation and digital tools to work for agricultural decision-making. From October 14 to 17, 2025, the project ran the SEEDS Seminar Series: four days of talks on remote sensing and AI for agriculture and food security. It was held online and hosted by the Department of Geographical Sciences, University of Maryland. Speakers came from NASA Harvest, NASA Acres, Harvard and the University of Montana.
